REFERENCE BY THE CHAIR 
75TH ANNIVERSARY OF DANDI MARCH 
MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: As the hon. Members are aware, on the 12th 
March, 2005, the nation celebrates the 75th Anniversary of the Dandi March. On 
this historic occasion, the Father of the Nation, Mahatma Gandhi, along with 
several patriotic volunteers, challenged the imposition of Salt Tax by the British 
Government. The non-violent protest through the medium of Salt Satyagraha 
had an appeal across regional, class and ethnic boundaries throughout the 
country. 
On this occasion, we pay homage to the memory of the Father of the Nation 
and the non-violent Satyagrahis whose heroic efforts contributed towards the 
independence of the country.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Banned medicines 
*141. SHRI SHAHID SIDDIQUI: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the fact that many medicines, used in 
India, are banned abroad for a long time; 
(b) if so, the details of those medicines alongwith their names; and 
(c) whether Government have taken any action to ban them in India; if so, the 
details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI 
RAMDOSS): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 

RAJYA SABHA [11 March, 2005] 
Statement 
There is no system of global banning of drugs. Certain drugs and 
formulations withdrawn in one or more countries may continue to be 
marketed in other countries. The decision to ban a drug by the regulatory 
authorities is normally based on the risk assessment process which is 
influenced by a number of factors such as disease pattern in a country, 
indications and dosages of the drug permitted, varying reactions of certain ethnic 
groups in a given population, availability of safer substitutes and overall safety 
profile of the drug. It is a well-known fact that administration of any drug is not 
absolutely free from side effects or adverse reactions in a statistically 
insignificant minority of the population. 
There is an adequate mechanism in India to review the status of the drug 
formulation as and when any serious adverse event is reported in the 
International journals, WHO Newsletters or when a drug formulation is 
reported to have been withdrawn in some countries. The use of the drug, so 
reported, is assessed in consultation with the experts, based on available 
technical information, benefit-risk ratio, local needs etc. The matter is further 
considered by the Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB), a statutory body 
under the Drugs & Cosmetics Act, 1940. 
Seventy six categories of drug formulations have so far been prohibited in the 
country by the Central Government, which were considered irrational or 
harmful in the context of present knowledge. In the recent past, drugs like 
Astemizole, Terfinadine and Rofecoxib have been prohibited after due 
assessment of their benefit-risk ratio by the experts, while drugs like Analgin, 
Hydroxyquinoline, Furazolidone, Phenylpropanolamine, Nimesulide etc. have 
been permitted to be continued to be marketed after due examination of their 
safety and use in the country. 
A National Pharmacovigilance Programme has been launched in 2004 to 
capture data on adverse reactions to drug use in the country.

SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, I would like to 
know from the hon. Minister about the standards of drug research in India. And, if 
they are not of international standard, what are the steps contemplated by the 
Government of India for strengthening drug research in India so that they could be on 
a par with the international standards? Has any research or investigation been initiated 
for drugs which are banned abroad, but are available in the Indian market and are 
being used by our countrymen? 
DR. ANBUMANI RAMDOSS: Sir, Indian R&D industry is growing at a 
rapid pace and competing with the worl d market. We could proudly say that 
the Indian R&D today is one of the bests in the world. And, equally, the 
Government is trying to regulate it so that more ethical issues and ethical 
standards could be put into research. And, it is not that people who come to India 
do research and after clinical trials get away. We have our own National Ethical 
Council through the ICMR, we have our own State regulatory bodies, we have 
the National Pharmaco Vigilance Committee which has been constituted 
recently to curb these practices or malpractices in drugs and research. 
Coming to the second part of the question which relates to the drugs which 
are banned in other countries, but are being used in our country, I would like to 
say, Sir, that no drug is globally banned. And there is no organisation which can 
ban a drug globally. Decisions with regard to banning of drugs are taken at the 
highest level in each and every country, where it is marketed or manufactured. 
Like, if a drug is banned by the FDA in America, it is not automatically banned in 
other countries. There are different issues like drugs could be metabolised 
differently between different individuals and between different ethnic groups. 
For example, Sir, drug 'A' could be metabolised very quickly in Shri Jairam 
Ramesh. ...(Interruptions).. The same drug could be metabolised very slowly in 
Mr. Narayanasamy, although both have the same body mass. In Indian people, 
drugs can be metabolised very fast. The same drug could be metabolised very 
slowly in white people. So there are di fferent issues. It is not like automatic 
banning. In India, we have our own e xperts, we have our own Drug Technical 
Advisory Board, National Pharmaco Vigilance Committee, to look into each 
and every issue of drugs being banned and according to merits we go about it.

Statement 
Cholera, viral hepatitis, enteric fever and acute diarrhoeal diseases are the main 
water borne diseases caused by contamination of water with virus, bacteria 
parasites. The number of patients suffering from these water, borne diseases during 
the period from 2002 to 2004, State/Union Territory-wise and disease-wise is 
annexed as Statement-I (See below). The relevant data on the rural-urban basis is 
not centrally maintained. 
Health is primarily a State subject and provision of medical relief for water 
borne diseases like cholera etc. through primary and community health centres 
is looked after by the State Government. Unsafe drinking water, poor sanitation 
and hygiene are some of the causes of water borne diseases. The preventive 
measures taken by the local health authorities include privision of safe 
drinking water, improvement of personnel and community hygiene, safe 
disposal of human excreta, undertak ing appropriate health education, 
surveillance and monitoring, distribution of chlorine tablets and ORS packets 
etc. 
The Government of India supplements the efforts of the State 
Government/Union Territories by providing funds under the Accelerated Rural 
Water Supply Programme,  Accelerated Urban Water Supply Programme, 
Total Sanitation Campaign,School Sanitation and Hygiene Education and Low 
Cost Sanitation Scheme for tackling quality related problems is respect of 
rural and urban drinking water supply. National Institute of Communicable 
Diseases, Delhi (NICD) provides techni cal support to the State Governments 
and undertake surveillance, early detection and prevention and control of 
outbreaks of communicable diseases including water borne diseases. Technical 
support to improve the quality of drinking water is also envisaged to be 
provided by NICD, Delhi. 
The Government of India has launched an Integrated Disease Surveillance 
Programme in November, 2004, to further strengthen identification of 
outbreaks of various diseases including water-borne diseases like Typhoid, 
Cholera, Jaundice etc. So that ear ly intervention could be made and 
occurrence, disability and death due to various diseases could be reduced.

Statement 
(a) The funds for implementation of National AIDS Control Programme 
Phase II are provided in lump sum to all the AIDS Control Societies and anti-
AIDS drugs are part of this. Statement-I indicating release of funds to all the 
State AIDS Control Societies (SACS) during the last three years is annexed.

(b) Yes, Sir. Anti-AIDS drugs are provided free of charge through 25 ART 
Centres established in selected Government medical institutions in 13 States of 
the country. The Anti Retroviral drugs used for treatment of AIDS patients 
through these ART Centers are the triple drug combination generic drugs 
manafactured by pharmaceutical companies based in India. The triple drug 
combination for AIDS patients not having TB include

quality of life and longevity of AIDS patients but do not cure HIV/AIDS 
completely. 
(c) National AIDS Control Programme for prevention and control of HIV/ 
AIDS is a comprehensive programme .-and is being implemented in the country 
through 35 State AIDS Control Societies and 3 AIDS Control Societies run by 
the municipal corporations in cities like Mumbai, Chennai and Ahmedabad. The 
programme is  focused on: (i) Intensive IEC (Information, Education and 
Communication) for general population with behaviour change communication 
for high risk groups; (ii) voluntary counseling and testing facilities; (iii) 
provision of safe blood; (iv) control of Sexually transmitted infections through 
STI Clinics and an aggressive condom promotion campaign; (v) establishing 
centres for Prevention of Parents to Child Transmission (PPTCT) and (vi) 
Providing care and support services to people living with HIV/AIDS, 
treatment facilities for Opportunistic Infections in all the Government medical 
colleges and district hospitals, community care centers, Drop-in-Centers and 
provision of free Anti Retroviral drugs through selected Government hospitals.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) to (d) A Joint Group was constituted by 
the Government under the Chairmanship of an Add itional Secretary in the 
Ministry of Agriculture with the following terms of reference:— 
(i) To review the status position of existing Crop Insurance Schemes i.e. 
National Agricultural Insurance Scheme  (NAIS), Pilot Project on Farm 
Income Insurance Scheme (FIIS), Varsha Bima Yojana and other agriculture 
related schemes floated by Private General Insurance Companies. 
(ii) Improvements requird in National Agricultural Insurance Scheme. 
(iii) To develop broad parameters/concept paper of an appropriate and 
farmers friendly crop insurance sche me after taking into account of 
professional inputs obtained from experts and private sector general 
insurance companies. 
(iv) To make assessment of up front subsidy, if any, to be paid by the 
government. 
The Group has submitted its report on 20.12.2004. The major 
recommendations of the Group relating to the Crop Insurance are:- 
* Reduction in the unit area of insurance to the level of village 
Panchayat for major crops. 
* Threshold/guaranteed yield is proposed to the based on best 5 years 
out of preceding 7 years yield data. 
* Indemnity levels will be 90% for low risk areas/crops and 80% for 
other areas/crops. 
* Coverage of pre-sowing/planning risks (i.e. prevented sowing on 
account of adverse seasonal cond itions). The indemnity payable 
may range between 20% - 25% of sum insured. 
* Post-harvest losses on account of cyclone are to be covered in 
coastal areas for a period of two weeks from harvesting provided the 
harvested crop is lying in the field. 
63 

RAJYA SABHA [11 March, 2005] 
* Uniform seasonality discipline for loanee and non-loanee farmers is 
to be followed in consultation with the States/UTs. 
* On account payment of claims is to be made during the season on 
the basis of weather data or satellite imagery of other proxy 
indicators so as to make timely payment of claims. 
* An individual assessment of claims will be carried out in case of 
specified localized calamities viz. hailstorm, landslide and damage 
due to wild animals. 
* Insurance scheme to be placed on actuarial regime. However, the 
premium to be paid by the farmers be suitably subsidized. 
* AIC should expand its network in terms of district level franchise, 
rural agents, micro-insurance agents to provide better service to 
farmers, particularly non-loanee farmers.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) Setting up of Agricultural Markets is a 
State subject. In the existing law dealing with agricultural marketing (APMC 
Act) the State Government alone is empowered to initiate the process of 
setting up of markets for agricultural commodities in notified areas. The 
processing industry cannot buy directly from the farmers. The farmer is 
restricted from entering into direct c ontract with any manufacturer as the 
produce is required to be canalized  through regulated markets. These 
restrictions are acting as disincentive to farmers, trade and industries. The 
State Governments have, therefore, been advised to bring reforms to the 
APMC Act to allow direct marketing and contract farming and to permit 
setting up of competitive markets in private and cooperative sectors. 
(b) No, Sir. The aim of the reforms is to develop alternative competitive 
markets in private and cooperative sectors so as to provide freedom to farmer 
to sell his produce in the market pr oviding better prices/services. These 
markets would operate in addition to existing structure of regulated markets.

organized at New Delhi on 7.1.2004 and at Bangalore on 19.11.2004 in order 
to evolve a consensus on the reforms required in the agricultural marketing 
sector.

reforms in the Agricultural Marketing s ector. The States of Madhya Pradesh, 
Maharashtra, Karnataka, Uttar Prades h and Punjab have already amended 
their APMC Act/Rules for promoting contract farming and direct marketing 
and/or for permitting private and cooperative investments etc. for setting up 
of agricultural markets.

1112. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that drugs containing Phenyl Propanol Amine 
(PPA) for nasal decongestion and considered prone to stroke are banned in 
many parts of world but are freely sold in the country; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the steps being taken to minimize effect of such formulations in anti-
cold pills to prevent stroke? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (c) The 
PPA (Phenylpropanolamine) has been used in cough and cold preparations in 
many countries. The PPA containing products were withdrawn in USA in 
November 2000, where these were marketed in higher strengths for weight 
loss in addition to their use in cough and cold preparations. These were 
withdrawn because of a reported risk of Hemorrhagic Stroke indicated by a 
study conducted in Yale University. The Committee on Safety of Medicines 
in UK also examined the safety of PPA  and concluded that the evidence of 
link between Hemorrhagic Stroke and PPA was weak and the formulations 
for cough and cold in low doses could continue to be sold in UK. 
The matter was also simultaneously ex amined in India in 2000-2001 in 
consultation with the experts and it was felt that in view of the similarity of 
use of PPA formulations in India to that of UK, the drug should be permitted 
to be marketed in cough and cold preparation with daily dose not more than 
50mg for children and 10Omg for adults.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (c)

In order to eradicate Polio, Governme nt has taken effective measures by

117 

RAJYA SABHA [11 March, 2005] 
Under the Universal Immunization Programme (UIP), vaccines are given 
to the children for protection against 6 preventable diseases of measles, 
diphtheria, pertussis, tuberculosis, tetanus and polio. UIP is implemented by 
the States. 
TUBERCULOSIS: 
To control TB, National Tuberculosis Control Programme (NTCP) was 
launched in the country in 1962. NTCP could not achieve the desired results. 
Therefore, Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP), widely 
known as DOTS which is a WHO recommended strategy is being 
implemented since 1997 in a phased manner with the objective of achieving 
cure rate of 85% of new sputum positive cases and to detect at least 70% of 
such cases, diagnosis by sputum microscopy instead of X-ray helps in 
detecting infectious cases and monitoring their treatment on priority. 
Facilities for diagnosis by sputum micr oscopy have been decentralized and 
strengthened. Drugs are provided free of cost in patient-wise boxes and 
consumed by the patients under direct observation of the DOT provider and 
patients are regularly monitored so that they complete their treatment. 
Presently, more than 950 million population in 547 districts/reporting units 
have been covered under the revised strategy. The Project districts have 
reported cure rate of more than 85% which means that more than 8 out of 
every 10 patients put on treatment under the revised strategy are being 
successfully cured as against below 4 in the earlier programme. To make the 
programme more accessible to larger se gments of the population, and to 
supplement the Government efforts in this direction, emphasis is being given 
to involve the community, medical colleges, all general hospitals, private 
practitioners and NGOs in the programme. 
MALARIA, DENGUE AND KALA-AZAR: 
The Govemment of India implementing comprehensive National Vector 
Borne Diseases Control Programme (N VBDCP) in the entire country for 
prevention and control of vector borne diseases namely Malaria, Filaria, Kala-
azar, Japanese Encephalitis and Dengue . The Government of India provide 
technical support, drugs for treatment of Malaria, Kala-azar and Dengue. 
Insecticides and Larvicides are also provided to the States as per the approved 
pattern. Assistance is provided for training programme and IEC. State 
Governments are responsible for planning, implementation and monitoring of 
the programme. 
Overall incidence of malaria in the country has declined from 2.08 million 
118 

[11 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
cases in 2001 to 1.72 million in 2004 (as per information received from the 
States). It is globally accepted that Malaria eradication is not technically 
feasible. Therefore, it has been envisa ged in the National Health Policy to 
reduce its morbidity and mortality by 50% by the year 2010. The National 
Health Policy also envisaged eliminati on of Kaia-azar by the year 2010. The 
following strategies are being adopted to prevent and control Malaria, Kala-
azar and Dengue:— 
A. Malaria: 
• Early Diagnosis and prompt treatment of malaria cases. 
• Integrated vector control. 
Early Detecton and Containment of malaria outbreak. 
• Information, Education and Communication (IEC) for personal 
protection and community involvement for malaria control. 
• Training and Capacity Building of Medical and Para-medical 
workers. 
• Monitoring and evaluation. 
• Efficient Management Information System (MIS). 
B. Kala-azar: 
• Early diagnosis and complete treatment through Primary Health 
Care System. 
• Interruption of transmission through vector control by undertaking 
residual insecticidai spraying in affected areas. 
• Health Education and Community Participation. 
C. Dengue: 
• Epidemiological surveillance of Dengue cases. 
• Entomological surveillance of aedes aegypti mosquitoes. 
• Clinical management of reported cases. 
• Control of mosquitoes through integrated vector management 
including source reduction, use of larvivorous fish. 
• Impregnated bednets and selective fogging with Pyrethrum.

Health Improvement Programme 
1176.   DR. KARAN SINGH: 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the recent study on social progress and outlook made by World 
Bank shows that health indicators in India have not exactly improved and 
shows a mixed bag of results; 
(b) if so, whether according to the study various reasons have been 
mentioned in its survey report; 
(c) whether Government have considered this study report of the World 
Bank regarding the health progress; and 
(d) if so, what are the main  steps that are being considered to improve the 
health programmes as suggested by the survey report? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) 
According to recent study on social progress and outlook made by the World 
Bank, there has been a progressive improvement in certain health indicators, 
viz, life expectancy at birth, Infant Mo rtality Rate (IMR) and malnourished 
children, over last two decades. Howeve r, there is a deterioration in health 
indicators like Maternal Mortality Rate (MMR) and prevalence of HIV. 
(c) and (d) The Report of the World Bank has been considered. The report 
itself has qualified that there are probl ems with the data for the indicator 
(MMR) in some of the largest States that raised questions regarding data at 
the national level. The report of the National Family Health Survey-ll also 
acknowledges that the di fference in the estimate s of MMR of NFHS-I and 
NFHS-II is not statistically significant due to various reasons such as larger 
sampling errors etc. The Sample Regist ration System (SRS) of the Registrar 
General of India have estimated the MMR for the country as 407 per 1,00,000 
live births in 1998 which is the same  period when NFHS-II have estimated 
the MMR as 540 per 1,00,000 live births. It is thus not correct to say that the 
material mortality rate has worsened. 
It is true that the estimated number of HIV infections in the country has 
risen from 3.5 million infections in 1998 to 5.1 million infections in 2003. 
Reasons for rise in HIV positive person s are low awareness of people about 
HIV/AIDS in the country especially rural and female partners in the highly 
vulnerable States; high proportion of migrant population; inadequate 
145 

RAJYA SABHA [11 March, 2005] 
safe sex practices; and large number of vulnerable population. 
In order to accelerate decline of Maternal Mortality Rate, provision has 
been made for upgrading Primary Health Centres for providing 24-hour 
delivery services, operationalising the First Referral units for providing 
Emergency Obsteric Care and training the health staff for providing Skilled 
J3irth Attendance at delivery, under the Second phase of Reproductive and 
Child Health Programme. 
In order to prevent and control th e spread of HIV/AIDS in India, 
Government has launched a comprehensive National AIDS Control 
Programme, currently under implementation throughout the country as a 
centrally sponsored scheme with following components:— 
• Preventive interventions for high-risk populations through targeted 
interventions adopting a multi-pronged strategy including peer 
counselling and behaviour change; 
• Preventive interventions for the general population through 
programmes for blood safety, voluntary counselling and testing 
services, Prevention of Parent to Child Transmission (PPTCT), 
Information Education and Communication (IEC); 
• Provision of low cost care and support services by providing 
community care services, treatment of opportunistic infections and 
prevention of occupational exposure; 
• Collaborative efforts to promote inter-sectoral programme activities 
including workplace interventions and public private partnerships; 
• Build technical and managerial capacities for programme 
implementation through surveillance, training, monitoring and 
evaluation, technical resource gr oups, operational research and 
programme management.

Cancer 
1191. SHRIMATI S.G. INDIRA. Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India has the World's highest incidence of 
cancer of the gall bladder, mouth and lower pharynx; 
157 

RAJYA SABHA [11 March, 2005] 
(b) whether it is also a fact that accord ing to a report, thyroid cancer has 
been detected in women in the coastal districts of Kerala, Karnataka and Goa; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that said report had highlighted and confirmed 
earlier observation that the breast cance r has replaced cervical cancer as the 
leading site of cancer among women in Indian cities and that lung cancer is 
the common cancer in various metropolitan cities in the country; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and the action Government propose to 
reduce the changing risk of cancer? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (d) 
According to the Cancer Atlas brought out by Indian Council of Medical 
Research (ICMR) based on data collected under the National Cancer Registry 
Programme (NCRP), the incidence of different cancers is not uniform 
throughout the country. While cancer inci dence in India as a whole is much 
lower in comparison to the incidence across the world, the incidence cancers 
of mouth, tongue and gall bladder in the country is higher than those reported 
in the "Cancer Incidence of 5 Continents" published by WHO in 2002. As per 
the Atlas on the basis of ICMR's population based cancer registry data, the 
highest incidence rates have been reported for the cancer of gall bladder 
among the women in Delhi and the cancer of tongue and mouth among the 
men in Bhopal. The highest rate of cancer of lower Pharynx as reported from 
Aizwal is based on the inputs from the Collaborative Centres which include 
private hospitals as well. 
(b) According to the Cancer Atlas, th yroid cancer has been detected in the 
coastal areas of Kerala, Karnataka and Goa. Breast cancer among women is 
one of the leading cancers in urban areas  whereas lung cancer is not the most 
common cancer in the Metropolitan cities in India. 
In order to control this problem, National Cancer Control programme was 
launched in 1975 with the objectives  of prevention, early detection and 
treatment of cancer in the country. The strategies under the program me are 
awareness generation in the community for prevention and early detection of 
cancer, and provision of comprehensive cancer treatment facilities across the 
country byway of supporting Regional Cancer Centres. Government Medical 
Colleges and Government Hospitals are also supported by Development of 
Oncology Wings.

Steel Prices 
1223. SHRI SANJAY NIRUPAM: Will the Minister of STEEL be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether prices of steel has gone up and there is a big hike likely to 
happen in March, 2005; 
(b) if so, the details about the price rise and its impact upon the raw 
materials; and 
(c) the steps being taken by Government to check the price rise? 
THE MINISTER OF STEEL (SHRI RAM VILAS PASWAN): (a) Yes, 
Sir. The steel prices have gone up in the last two years. However, the World 
Steel Dynamics has estimated that, around 22 million tonnes of new steel 
capacity has been commissioned around the world and has also predicted that 
China may soon turn into a net exporter of steel. Under such circumstances a 
'big hike' in steel prices in the near future is unlikely. 
(b) The details of steel prices of some important steel items at four metros 
in February, 2004 and February, 2005 is given in the Statement (See below). 
The raw material input prices required for steel making have also increased in 
tandem with the rise in price of finished steel. 
(c) While prices are determined by the interplay of market forces, 
Government has been taking various steps to ensure both adequate 
availability and stability in prices of steel in the domestic market. The 
measures taken by the Government inter-alia include considerable reduction 
in import duties on steel as well as steel making inputs, reduction in DEPB 
rates on steel items and fixation of value caps for all items of iron and steel 
and ferro alloys, increasing allocation of  iron and steel materials for the SSI 
sector and advising steel PSUs to export only after fulfilling the domestic 
requirement.

Need to increase the Service Tax Net 
SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA (Andhra Pradesh) : 'Services' constitute a very 
heterogeneous spectrum of economic activities. Over a period of time, the 
definition 'Service' has also undergone a ch ange. In any Welfare State, if is the 
primary responsibility of the Government  to fulfil the increasing developmental 
needs of the country and its people by way of public expenditure. India, being a 
developing economy, is striving to fulfil t he obligations of a Welf are State within its 
limited resources. The service sector is now occupying the centre stage of 
economy; so much so, in the contempora ry world, development of service sector 
has become synonymous with the advancement  of economy. As we know that the 
Government's primary sources of revenue ar e direct and indirect taxes. Apart from 
getting revenue, the Government also wish to raise employment opportunities in 
service sector. With this view, the Gove rnment of India imposed Service Tax on 
some services which cover a range of activities -management, banking, insurance, 
hospitality, administration, communication, entertainment, wholesale distribution 
and retailing including R&D activities. 
196 

[11 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Presently, there are 71 services operating in India. But the Government of 
India has not included services like legal and medial which are available only 
against huge payment, and the Government is not getting any revenue on the 
services rendered by them. Hence I request, that the Government should 
impose Service Tax on the above professions and on similar other professions 
which will help to generate more revenue that can then be used to make this. 
country a welfare State. I also request to have a single window mechanism for 
Service Tax in avoiding computational difficulties. 
Accord of Central Approval for Cauvery Water Supply Scheme for 
Bangalore City 
SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD (Karnataka): Sir, to cope with the growing 
demand in Bangalore Urban conglomeration area, the Government of 
Karnataka has proposed to augment the existing water supply capacity by an 
additional 540 million litres a day, under  the Cauvery Water Supply Scheme 
Stage IV, Phase II. 
Due to erratic monsoons for years in a row and depleting ground 
water resources, it is imperative that a public utility project of this nature and 
magnitude should be in place to cater to the growing demand for potable water 
supply. 
As a major component of the Stat e's multi-pronged strategy to 
augment water supply to Bangalore urban area, the Cauvery Water Supply 
Scheme in its present phase assumes pr iority. The State Government has 
already listed this project for its current fiscal year 2004-05 and is awaiting the 
clearance of the Department of Economic Affairs, Government of India. 
I urge upon the Centre to accord its clearance for this project of 
utmost utility and urgency along with concomitant financial package. 
Need for distinction between AIDS/HIV and other cases of immune 
deficiencies 
SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, 
India is the second most affected country in the world as far as prevalence of 
HIV/AIDS is concerned. We  are spending thousands of crores of rupees on 
antiretroviral drugs, drug therapy, aware ness, etc. to prevent this pandemic. 
We are also spending huge amounts of money on awareness because this is 
the important means through which we can reduce this menace since there is 
no cure to this deadly disease. We have started in January this year the 'Red 
Ribbon Express' as a part of Our awareness 
197 

RAJYA SABHA         [11 March, 2005] 
campaign. In spite of taking severa l measures, health functionaries at 
grassroots are not able to distingu ish between Acquired Immuno Deficiency 
Syndrome and Human Immunodeficiency Virus, on the one hand, and other 
cases of immune deficiency, on the other,  to minimise the stigma associated 
with AIDS in the absence of a clear-cut  definition, and they are clubbing all 
cases of immune deficiency together. As a result, even those who suffer from 
it -- because of other causes -- are fa cing the stigma and discrimination and 
women, in particular, are the worst affected. So, the Government of India 
should review the manner in which HIV/AIDS surveys were conducted to 
ensure that they do not include case s of immune deficiency caused by other 
factors with HIV/AIDS. At the same ti me, Gol should also make it clear, 
through awareness campaigns that not all cases of HIV develop into AIDS. I 
also request that names of Central a nd State AIDS organisations should be 
changed since they are not just dealing with AIDS cases but also with other 
cases.

Repair and renovation of Hirakud Canal System in Orissa 
MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR (Orissa): Sir, the Hirakud Dam Project over 
the river Mahanadi in Orissa is one of  the largest post-Independence projects. 
It is meant for hydro-electricity generation and irrigation. The canal system 
from the reservoir of Hirakud runs for ab out 125 kilometres in length, covering 
six districts of Orissa. The canals ar e meant to irrigate one lakh fifty-five 
thousand six hundred and fifty hectares of agricultural land in the command 
area. 
The Hirakud Dam Project was completed in 1957. It had been 
inaugurated on 13 th January, 1957 by the first Prime Minister of India, Pandit 
Nehru. The canal system started operat ing from 1961. Now, during the last 
over 40 years, the canal system has se rved the area .well; the districts of 
Sambalpur and Bargarh are considered the rice bowl of Orissa. However, the 
canal system has not got repaired and renovated due to various reasons. This 
has resulted in less flow of water to the tail-end. This has also caused drop in 
the area of irrigation by 20 to 25 per cent during Khariff crop and 25 to 30 per 
cent during the Rabi crop, This has adversely affected the economy of the 
farmers. 
Sir, I request the Government to take up renovation of the canal 
system of Hirakud irrigation network through the Central Water Resources

Ministry. The Government may cons ider adequate support to the State 
Government in this regard also so that  periodic maintenance of the irrigation 
system could be done to make the life of the farmers easy.

Pending cases in various courts in the country 
SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA (Andhra Pr adesh): Sir, I would like to 
draw the attention of the Union Government towards the pending cases in 
various courts of the country. It is very unfortunate that over the years so many 
cases have accumulated in the courts a nd it inevitably highlights the saying, 
'justice delayed is justice denied'. 
Sir, the Annual Report of the year 2003-04 of the Ministry of Law and 
Justice highlights these facts. Accord ing to that Report, there are about 
2,28,00,000 cases which are pending in va rious courts of our country. About 
20 crore people are involved in these cases, and the time consumed on these 
cases, apart from money involved cannot be explained. 
Sir, on the initiative of the De partment of Justice, the Finance 
Commission is reported to have recommended a scheme for creation of 1734 
additional courts in the country fo r disposing of long-pending cases, 
particularly those cases which have been pending for more than two years 
199 

RAJYA SABHA                      [11 March, 2005] 
and those cases in which undertrials are in  jails. At present, it is stated that 
there are about two lakh undertrials in various jails. About eighteen per cent of 
them have been in jails' for more than one year. By the end of 2004, 1652 Fast 
Track Courts are reported to have be en established and which have disposed 
of 3,70,504 cases. 
Sir, in a judgment, the Supreme Cour t has emphasised that this huge 
accumulation of undecided cases in the courts has been due to inadequate 
strength of judges as compared to the population. The judge strength ratio in 
India is stated to be 10.5 per 10 lakh people. The Supreme Court is of the view 
that the strength of judges should, in  the first instance, be increased to 50 
judges for 10 lakh people, and that this increase should be effected in the next 
two-three years in all the States, and appointment of judges and magistrates 
should be effected without any delay. Hence, I request the Union Government 
to expedite the above process in the larger interest of the people.

Concern over abduction of school children in the country 
DR. (SHRIMATI) NAJMA A. HEPTU LLA (Rajasthan): Mr. Vice-
Chairman. Sir, innocent school children  are increasingly becoming the target 
of criminal gangs who have turned to kidnapping-for-a-ransom - this could well 
be the only booming business in some States. In Kishlay's case, his parent as 
well as the police said no ransom had been paid. However, in the past, victims 
have hardly ever got out of the clutches of abductors without paying a ransom. 
The gangs pick them up without much difficulty and the money is very 
good; parents are only too ready to pay any sum for the release of their child. 
The modus operandi is professional. The target is chosen after a lot of 
investigation. A very motivated gang identified targets. The police revealed 
that a separate group identified the pe rson. All vital information on assets, 
income, connections with the powers that be and the rout ine are the gang's 
much needed data. 
Earlier in Bihar, only a few big gangs were on the scene. Soon the 
gangs increased - kidnapping became a very lucrative affair. Money could be 
made with ease. Unemployment and eas y availability of arms has attracted 
many youths. Nowadays, one gang may not be involved in a particular 
abduction. In some recent cases, the police have found that a victim may be 
passed on from the gang to another, sometimes even to gangs in other States. 
Police registered 32,085 cases of kidna pping from 1992 to September 2004 in 
Bihar, which accounts for 26.5 per cent of  India's total reported crimes. Many 
abductions are not reported as families often prefer to deal with the kidnappers 
directly to try to ensure the victim's
